query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Degradation of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy at elevated temperatures is primarily governed by the selective oxidation behavior of reactive elements. Under oxidizing gases, rapid surface diffusion of Cr (and a minor contribution from Al) leads to the formation of a coherent, thin dual-layer oxide (Cr2O3 and Al2O3) that protects the underlying fcc matrix. Under reducing conditions, the lack of sufficient oxygen prevents formation of a stable protective scale, resulting instead in incomplete surface oxidation and localized internal oxidation—particularly near grain boundaries—where depletion of Cr and Al promotes the nucleation of brittle Ti-rich or other intermetallic precipitates.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy exhibiting a single-phase fcc matrix with a homogeneous distribution of elements and no preformed oxide scale.
generation.intervention: Expose identical alloy samples to elevated-temperature environments (around 800°C) in two different gas atmospheres: (a) an oxidizing environment (e.g., air or oxygen-enriched gas) and (b) a reducing environment (e.g., a controlled CO/H2 gas mixture).
generation.conditions: Temperature ~800°C, exposure durations ranging from 100 to 500 hours, with the gas atmosphere strictly controlled for either oxidizing (O2 partial pressure near or above ambient air levels) or reducing conditions (O2 partial pressure significantly below ambient, e.g., <0.1%).
generation.structural_mediator: The stable fcc matrix of the alloy, which enables uniform elemental diffusion and determines how easily a protective oxide scale can form or be bypassed by internal oxidation processes.
generation.mechanism: In oxidizing conditions, the high mobility of Cr and modest contribution from Al favors the rapid formation of a continuous and adherent Cr2O3/Al2O3 scale that limits further oxygen ingress and preserves the alloy's mechanical integrity. In reducing conditions, the lower oxygen availability hinders the formation of such a protective scale, allowing internal oxidation to occur—this results in local depletion of protective elements and promotes the formation of brittle, potentially Ti-rich intermetallics at grain boundaries without altering the bulk fcc phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to oxidizing conditions will show a thin, uniform, and adherent oxide scale with limited underlying internal oxidation, thereby largely preserving strength and fatigue performance. Conversely, samples in reducing conditions will develop a patchy and thicker oxide layer accompanied by evidence of internal oxidation and formation of localized brittle phases at the grain boundaries, leading to degradation in mechanical properties over time.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated, homogeneous fcc alloy with no pre-existing oxide scale and high strength and fatigue performance, ideally maintained in an inert atmosphere.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable at temperatures around 800°C and for exposure durations sufficient to allow measurable oxide scale evolution (100–500 hours). Gas compositions must be distinctly oxidizing (e.g., air or oxygen-enriched) versus strongly reducing (e.g., CO/H2 mixture with very low oxygen partial pressure).
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative differences in oxide scale thickness, the precise composition of the dual-layer scale, and the degree of internal oxidation or brittle precipitate formation are uncertain due to the complex synergistic interactions among the multiple elements in this high-entropy alloy and possible effects of residual stresses from additive manufacturing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy samples. Group A will be exposed to an oxidizing atmosphere (air or oxygen-enriched gas) at 800°C for 300 hours, and Group B will be exposed to a reducing atmosphere (a controlled CO/H2 mixture with very low O2 partial pressure) under the same temperature and time. Pre- and post-exposure characterization should include surface and cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for oxide layer thickness and composition, X-ray diffraction (XRD) analyses for phase identification, and mechanical testing (e.g., fatigue and strength measurements).
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (via SEM/EDS)
Surface oxide composition (identifying Cr2O3, Al2O3, and any Ti-rich phases)
Internal microstructural changes (evidence of internal oxidation and precipitate formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidizing environment does not produce a thin, uniform, protective oxide scale or if the reducing environment does not lead to noticeably greater internal oxidation and evidence of localized brittle phase formation (or if both conditions show similar degradation behavior), then the hypothesis that selective oxidation kinetics (governed by reactive element diffusion) controls degradation would be falsified.
